chapters.title: An observation needs an interpretation and a control
chapters.formula: Observation -> possible explanations -> interference check -> confirmation
chapters.script: Welcome to Practical Chemistry. This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice. An observation in practical chemistry needs a chemical explanation and a check for alternatives. A precipitate, colour change or gas may support a conclusion, but its meaning depends on medium, concentration, reagent sequence and interfering species. Record what happened separately from the proposed identity. A white precipitate is an observation; assigning one particular salt is an interpretation that needs additional evidence. A blank or a comparison under matched conditions can reveal contamination or an interfering response. In an examination problem, combine every stated observation rather than guessing from one familiar colour. A valid identification must explain the full set of evidence. The later chapters connect this approach with titration ratios, selective precipitation, complexes, functional groups, crystallization and heat measurements. These are conceptual interpretations of stated experiments; the aim is to understand why an observation is expected and when it is inconclusive. A failed observation can also reflect inappropriate conditions rather than absence of the target species. Distinguish a useful clue from a uniquely identifying result, and use an independent confirmatory response when the evidence allows several explanations.
points: Observation · Colour / solid / gas · What happened
Interpretation · Possible species · Explain response
Confirmation · Selective extra evidence · Reject interference

board.heading: An observation needs an interpretation and a control

chapters.title: Titrations use stoichiometry at equivalence
chapters.formula: At equivalence: moles react in the balanced coefficient ratio
chapters.script: At equivalence, the reacted mole ratio follows the balanced equation. For monoprotic strong acid and monobasic strong base, the acid amount equals the base amount, so their concentration-volume products are equal. A diprotic acid requires the appropriate neutralization stage; do not assume every titration is one-to-one. An indicator endpoint is an observed signal near, but not identical by definition to, equivalence. Select an indicator whose transition suits the steep part of the titration curve. Use the delivered burette volume, not its final reading alone, and keep volume units consistent. Rinsing and parallax control help accuracy but cannot replace the balanced reaction. Twenty millilitres of zero point one zero zero mole per litre hydrochloric acid contains zero point zero zero two zero zero mole. At a one to one equivalence, the same amount of sodium hydroxide is needed. With a base concentration of zero point zero eight zero zero mole per litre, the required volume is twenty five millilitres. Equal moles here do not imply equal volumes.
points: Base concentration · Given · 0.0800 mol/L

board.heading: Titrations use stoichiometry at equivalence

chapters.title: Acidic permanganate ratios count electrons
chapters.formula: Acidic ratios: MnO4- : Fe2+ = 1:5; MnO4- : C2O4^2- = 2:5
chapters.script: Permanganate accepts five electrons when reduced to manganese two plus in suitable acidic medium. iron two plus supplies one electron each, giving one permanganate to five iron(II) ions. Oxalate supplies two electrons per oxalate ion as it becomes two carbon dioxide, giving two permanganate to five oxalate ions. The medium is essential: dilute sulfuric acid is commonly used in these titrations, whereas hydrochloric acid can introduce chloride oxidation and nitric acid can interfere as an oxidant. Permanganate serves as its own colour indicator through a slight persistent excess under suitable conditions. Oxalate oxidation has temperature and rate considerations, so observations are not just colour labels. Ten millilitres of zero point zero two zero zero mole per litre permanganate contains zero point zero zero zero two zero zero mole. Its five electron change corresponds to zero point zero zero one zero zero mole of iron two plus. Oxalate has a two electron change per ion, so two permanganates require five oxalates to balance ten electrons. Check the specified manganese product before applying either ratio.
points: Permanganate → Mn²⁺ · Accepts 5 · MnO₄⁻ : Fe²⁺ = 1:5
Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ · Gives 1 · Balance electrons
Oxalate → CO₂ · Gives 2 per ion · MnO₄⁻ : oxalate = 2:5

board.heading: Acidic permanganate ratios count electrons

chapters.title: Salt analysis depends on selective precipitation and complex formation
chapters.formula: A confirmatory test must be interpreted in its stated pH and chemical environment
chapters.script: Hydroxide precipitation, complex formation and controlled p H help distinguish listed cations. For example, copper two plus can show a blue hydroxide precipitate and a deep-blue ammine solution under suitable ammonia conditions. iron three plus can produce a reddish-brown hydroxide. Amphoteric aluminium and zinc hydroxides can dissolve in excess strong base, so precipitation alone does not uniquely separate them. Anion tests likewise need controls. A carbonate gives carbon dioxide on acidification; sulfate can give a white barium sulfate precipitate in an appropriately acidified test; halides can give silver salts after addressing interferences. Nitrite and nitrate differ in redox behaviour. These examples introduce the principles but do not replace the full scheme for every cation and anion listed by NTA. Copper and iron observations illustrate why solution environment matters. A precipitate can dissolve when a complex forms or when an amphoteric hydroxide reacts with excess base. Those changes are chemical evidence rather than a failure of precipitation. If aluminium and zinc both dissolve under one condition, another selective observation is needed to distinguish them. One shared response cannot uniquely identify either ion.
points: Deep-blue ammine · Copper(II) complex · Suitable ammonia medium
Reddish-brown hydroxide · Iron(III) · Confirm with context
Dissolves in excess base · Al / Zn hydroxides · Not unique identity

board.heading: Salt analysis depends on selective precipitation and complex formation

chapters.title: Functional-group tests have exceptions
chapters.formula: Multiple independent observations usually constrain identity better than one test
chapters.script: A suitable carbonyl reagent can identify many aldehydes and ketones, while Tollens' response supports an oxidizable substrate rather than uniquely proving every aldehyde. Phenolic groups can show characteristic complex or substitution reactions; a carboxylic acid commonly releases carbon dioxide from bicarbonate. An amine's class influences its identification chemistry. The iodoform test responds to suitable methyl-carbonyl compounds and precursors such as ethanol or isopropyl alcohol, not every alcohol. A negative result can arise from an unsuitable test environment. For a question involving several observations, intersect their structural implications and verify that the proposed compound satisfies all of them. Acetaldehyde is compatible with an aldehyde response and a positive iodoform response. Benzaldehyde can give an aldehyde oxidation response while lacking the methyl carbonyl pattern. A proposed structure must satisfy the intersection of the evidence. Also distinguish a true chemical exception from an observation affected by reagent condition, concentration or interference in the stated problem.
points: Acetaldehyde · Yes · Yes
Benzaldehyde · Yes · No
Interpretation · Combine responses · Check conditions

board.heading: Functional-group tests have exceptions

chapters.title: Preparation questions connect reaction with purification
chapters.formula: Mohr's salt: (NH4)2Fe(SO4)2 with 6H2O of crystallization; potash alum: KAl(SO4)2 with 12H2O
chapters.script: Mohr's salt is a hydrated double salt containing ammonium and iron(II) sulfate; potash alum is a hydrated potassium-aluminium sulfate double salt. Their preparation principles involve suitable solution chemistry and crystallization rather than inventing a new valence state from the word double. Oxidation of iron two plus and contamination are practical issues to consider. Named organic preparations include acetanilide, p-nitroacetanilide, aniline yellow and iodoform in the official scope. Acetylating aniline forms an amide, and nitration of acetanilide illustrates how a substituent affects aromatic orientation. Product separation, washing and purity checks matter alongside the reaction equation. Detailed reagent handling and recipes require a supervised manual. Crystallization water contributes to molar mass even though it does not change the named metal's oxidation state. Mohr's salt contains iron in the plus two state, whereas the aluminium in potash alum is plus three. In an organic preparation question, identify the intended functional group change and explain how purification separates product from impurities. A balanced equation alone does not establish the recovered material's purity.
points: Mohr salt · Iron in +2 state · 6 waters of crystallization
Potash alum · Aluminium in +3 state · 12 waters
Organic preparation · Functional-group change · Purification matters

board.heading: Preparation questions connect reaction with purification

chapters.title: Calorimetry measures the surroundings to infer reaction heat
chapters.formula: q_surroundings = (mc + C_cal) Delta T; q_reaction approximately -q_surroundings in the stated model
chapters.script: For a stated simple calorimeter model, heat gained by solution is mass times specific heat times temperature change; include the calorimeter heat capacity if supplied. If the reaction warms the surroundings, its heat is negative in that model. Divide by moles reacted to obtain a molar quantity, and state heat-loss or constant-pressure assumptions. The syllabus includes solution enthalpy of copper sulfate and neutralization enthalpy of a strong acid and base. Hydration state and concentration affect dissolution results, so anhydrous and hydrated samples cannot automatically share one value. Strong-acid/strong-base neutralization largely reflects water formation under dilute conditions, but dilution heats and heat losses can affect measured values. If one hundred grams of solution warms by two kelvin with specific heat four point one eight joules per gram per kelvin, it gains eight hundred thirty six joules. With negligible other heat capacity and losses, the reaction loses the same heat. For zero point zero two zero zero mole reacted, this is minus forty one point eight kilojoules per mole. Include a supplied calorimeter heat capacity before drawing that conclusion.
points: Solution heat · 100 × 4.18 × 2 · +836 J
Reaction heat · Opposite sign · −836 J

board.heading: Calorimetry measures the surroundings to infer reaction heat

chapters.title: Colloid and rate observations also need controlled conditions
chapters.formula: Clock comparison: rate proportional to 1/time only with the same defined threshold and suitable conditions
chapters.script: Lyophilic sols have stronger affinity between dispersed material and the medium than lyophobic sols in the elementary distinction. Stability and coagulation depend on the actual dispersion and electrolyte environment. Light scattering can reveal dispersed particles but does not alone identify the substance or prove the sample is a true solution. The iodide-hydrogen peroxide kinetic study connects reactant concentrations with the time or amount of iodine formation under specified conditions. Temperature, mixing and any threshold-detection system must be controlled. An inverse clock time can estimate relative rate only when the same product threshold and relevant conditions apply; it is not universally equal to a reaction-rate constant. For the same iodine threshold under comparable clock conditions, a twenty second time versus a forty second time corresponds to twice the average rate to that threshold. It does not by itself give an absolute rate constant. A different threshold, changed temperature or altered detection chemistry can invalidate the simple comparison. Identify the measured quantity before inferring a rate law from an experimental observation.
points: 20 s · Same threshold · 2
40 s · Same conditions · 1
Changed threshold · Not comparable directly · Reassess model

board.heading: Colloid and rate observations also need controlled conditions

chapters.title: Read a burette and subtract a blank
chapters.formula: Corrected titre = final reading − initial reading − blank
chapters.script: A titre is a delivered volume, not simply the final burette reading. Suppose the initial reading is three point one zero millilitres and the final reading twenty one point five zero. The delivered volume is eighteen point four zero millilitres. If a valid blank correction for the same analysis is zero point four zero millilitre, the corrected titre is eighteen point zero zero. For illustrative zero point zero two zero zero molar permanganate reducing to manganese two in acid, each mole accepts five electrons. Iron two becoming iron three supplies one electron per ion. The corrected amount therefore corresponds to zero point zero zero one eight zero mole of iron two. If that came from a twenty five point zero zero millilitre sample aliquot, its concentration is zero point zero seven two zero molar. State the reaction medium and use the appropriate electron factor. A blank correction addresses background consumption defined by the method; it is not an arbitrary adjustment to make repeated titres agree. Check delivered volume, correction sign, stoichiometry and sample volume as separate steps.
points: Delivered volume · 21.50 − 3.10 · 18.40 mL
Corrected titre · 18.40 − 0.40 · 18.00 mL

board.heading: Read a burette and subtract a blank

chapters.title: Distinguish uncertainty bounds from statistics
chapters.formula: For small worst-case relative bounds, add contributions in a product/ratio
chapters.script: A measurement uncertainty statement must identify whether it is a bound or a statistical estimate. For a concentration calculated as standard concentration times titre volume divided by sample volume, small worst case relative bounds add in a first order estimate. Suppose the standard concentration contributes zero point two zero percent, the titre zero point one zero percent and the sample volume zero point one five percent. The estimated worst case relative bound is zero point four five percent. At a central result zero point one zero zero zero molar, that corresponds to about zero point zero zero zero four five molar. This is not automatically a one standard deviation uncertainty or a ninety five percent confidence interval. Independent random standard uncertainties would use a different combination rule. Repeated close titres demonstrate precision under repeatability conditions; they do not by themselves remove calibration error or an incorrect endpoint. A consistent meniscus reading error can remain systematic across many trials. Match the reported significant figures to the actual uncertainty, and keep the meaning of the quoted error clear when comparing two analytical results.
points: Relative contributions · 0.20% + 0.10% + 0.15% · ≈0.45% worst-case bound
Repeated close results · Precision evidence · Not automatic accuracy

board.heading: Distinguish uncertainty bounds from statistics

chapters.title: Interpret confirmatory anion evidence
chapters.formula: Use a defined test scheme; one observation is not a universal identifier
chapters.script: Qualitative analysis builds a case from a defined sequence of observations and controlled interferences. In the standard carbonate comparison, acid treatment releases a gas that can turn limewater milky, consistent with carbon dioxide formation. Other acid reactive samples and gases require discrimination, so effervescence alone does not uniquely prove carbonate. A sulfate confirmation can involve a white barium sulfate precipitate that persists under the specified dilute acid conditions. For chloride, the familiar silver chloride precipitate is white and can dissolve in dilute aqueous ammonia under the appropriate test scheme. Those observations refer to different reagent systems; they must not be combined into one unlabelled result. Precipitation and complex formation can change what remains available for the next test. The meaning of an observation therefore depends on which aliquot, reagent and prior treatment produced it. Use the supplied method and comparison evidence rather than treating every white solid as the same substance. This chapter interprets analytical data and does not replace supervised laboratory handling, separation or disposal procedures.
points: Carbonate evidence · Gas; limewater response · Effervescence alone insufficient
Sulfate evidence · BaSO₄ precipitate · Persists in stated dilute acid
Chloride evidence · White AgCl; ammonia response · Interpret within defined scheme

board.heading: Interpret confirmatory anion evidence

chapters.title: Cation evidence includes complex formation
chapters.formula: Colour, precipitation and solubility are complementary observations
chapters.script: A cation can change its visible behaviour when its coordination environment changes. In a familiar copper two comparison, aqueous ammonia under suitable conditions can give a deep blue copper ammonia complex. Iron three with thiocyanate can give a strong red complex colour in the stated medium. These are useful pieces of evidence, not promises that colour alone identifies an arbitrary mixture. Concentration, acidity, competing ligands and other coloured species can affect what is observed. Aluminium hydroxide provides a different kind of evidence: its amphoteric behaviour allows dissolution in excess alkali through hydroxo species. Zinc hydroxide can also show amphoteric dissolution, so that observation is not unique to aluminium. Distinguish the original cation from the new precipitate or dissolved complex when explaining a result. A valid analysis often needs separation and more than one confirmation before assigning an ion. The purpose is to connect observed changes with equilibria and coordination chemistry, while retaining the limits of an individual test. Do not infer a complete systematic analysis from one familiar colour name.
points: Cu²⁺ with suitable NH₃ · Ammine complex · Deep blue evidence
Fe³⁺ with SCN⁻ · Complex formation · Red evidence
Al hydroxide in excess base · Amphoteric dissolution · Zn hydroxide can behave similarly

board.heading: Cation evidence includes complex formation

chapters.title: Include the vessel in a mixing heat balance
chapters.script: A mixing temperature calculation must account for every specified heat capacity and initial temperature. Mix one hundred grams of water at eighty degrees Celsius with two hundred grams at twenty degrees in a calorimeter initially at twenty degrees. Assume no heat loss, no phase change and constant water specific heat capacity four point two joules per gram kelvin. If the vessel heat capacity were negligible, the final temperature would be forty degrees Celsius. Now include a calorimeter heat capacity of eighty four joules per kelvin. This equals the heat capacity of twenty grams of water in the stated approximation. Heat lost by hot water equals heat gained by cold water and vessel. The weighted temperature is therefore eight thousand plus four thousand plus four hundred, divided by three hundred twenty, giving thirty eight point seven five degrees Celsius. The final temperature lies between the initial temperatures and is lower than the vessel free estimate because the vessel also warms. Do not include its heat capacity twice if a supplied combined calorimeter constant already contains the water contribution. State the insulation and constant heat capacity assumptions before treating the result as an experimental prediction.
points: Vessel heat capacity · 84/4.2 · 20 g water equivalent
Including vessel at 20 °C · 12400/320 · 38.75 °C

board.heading: Include the vessel in a mixing heat balance

chapters.title: Crystal recovery and purity are different measurements
chapters.formula: Recoverable mass = dissolved hot mass − mass left in cold mother liquor
chapters.script: Crystallization can separate material because solubility changes with temperature, but recovery is not a direct purity measurement. Consider supplied solubility data of twenty grams solute per one hundred grams water at the hot condition and five grams per one hundred grams water at the cold condition. Suppose ten grams of the target is fully dissolved in fifty grams water at the hot condition, then cooled without solvent loss. At the cold condition, fifty grams water can still hold two point five grams of target in solution. The ideal recovered crystal mass is therefore seven point five grams, or seventy five percent of the original target. This calculation assumes equilibrium solubilities, no target decomposition, no mechanical loss and the stated solvent mass throughout. Washing can remove adhering impurities but may also dissolve target, depending on the wash conditions. A higher recovered mass could include retained solvent or impurities rather than better recovery of pure material. A lower mass could reflect incomplete collection as well as solubility. Keep the mother liquor mass balance separate from evidence of chemical identity and purity; one percentage cannot establish all three conclusions.
points: Hot: 20 g per 100 g water · 50 g water holds 10 g · Initial target fully dissolved
Cold: 5 g per 100 g water · 50 g water retains 2.50 g · Mother-liquor target
Ideal recovered target · 10.0 − 2.50 = 7.50 g · 75.0% target recovery

board.heading: Crystal recovery and purity are different measurements

chapters.title: A hydrated salt standard needs its full formula mass
chapters.formula: Mohr’s salt: one Fe²⁺ per (NH₄)₂Fe(SO₄)₂·6H₂O formula unit
chapters.script: A weighed hydrated salt must be converted into amount using the formula actually supplied. Mohr's salt contains one iron two ion per formula unit together with ammonium, sulfate and six waters of crystallization. For an illustrative pure sample, use supplied formula mass three hundred ninety two grams per mole. Dissolving three point nine two grams to a final solution volume of two hundred fifty millilitres gives zero point zero one zero zero mole formula units and the same iron two amount. The formal iron concentration is zero point zero four zero zero molar. A twenty five point zero millilitre aliquot then contains zero point zero zero one zero zero mole iron two. Under a specified quantitative acidic permanganate reaction with five iron two ions per permanganate ion, that aliquot requires zero point zero zero zero two zero zero mole permanganate. At zero point zero two zero zero molar titrant, its volume is ten point zero millilitres. Ignoring the waters gives the wrong weighed-mass conversion. Oxidation of iron two or sample impurity can change an actual assay, so these predictions depend on the supplied purity and reaction conditions rather than on the salt name alone.
points: 25.0 mL aliquot · 0.00100 mol Fe²⁺ · Divide by 5 for MnO₄⁻
Titrant 0.0200 M · 0.000200 / 0.0200 L · 10.0 mL at stated endpoint

board.heading: A hydrated salt standard needs its full formula mass

chapters.title: A melting range is evidence rather than a unique identity
chapters.formula: Compare ranges under matching measurement conditions
chapters.script: A reported melting observation is usually a range, not a universal exact temperature from one glance. Suppose a reference crystalline material is supplied as melting from one hundred twenty one to one hundred twenty two degrees Celsius under the stated method. A sample melting across one hundred twelve to one hundred nineteen has a lower and broader range. That is consistent with impurity or other sample and measurement problems, but it does not identify a particular contaminant by itself. Heating rate, thermometer calibration, residual solvent, sample packing and decomposition can affect the observation. A sharp range matching a reference supports identity and purity when combined with other evidence; it does not prove them uniquely. Different compounds can have similar melting ranges, and some mixtures can show relatively sharp eutectic melting. A mixed melting point with a known reference can add evidence when the material and method are appropriate, but interpretation still needs care. If a thermometer has a stated positive one degree bias, correct the observed reading downward by one degree before comparison. Precision, calibration and a chemical conclusion are separate steps. State which observation changed and which possible explanations remain rather than replacing evidence with a memorized rule.
points: Reference range · 121–122 °C supplied · Compare matching method
Sample range · 112–119 °C observed · Lower and broader; not unique cause
Thermometer bias +1 °C · Correct observed value −1 °C · Calibration before interpretation

board.heading: A melting range is evidence rather than a unique identity
rows: Lower and broader; not unique cause

chapters.title: Coagulation evidence starts with the colloid charge
chapters.formula: The oppositely charged ion is the counter-ion in the elementary comparison
chapters.script: Colloid coagulation comparisons begin with the sign of the dispersed particles, not with memorizing one order of salt names. For a negatively charged sol, cations act as the counter ions in the elementary charge neutralization comparison. With otherwise comparable conditions, higher counter ion charge commonly increases coagulating power, although real systems also depend on specific ion chemistry and the medium. Suppose supplied critical coagulation concentrations are fifty millimolar sodium chloride, one millimolar magnesium chloride and zero point one millimolar aluminium chloride. Lower required concentration means stronger action in that measured comparison. Using reciprocal thresholds gives relative powers one, fifty and five hundred after normalization to the sodium salt. This is an interpretation of supplied data, not a universal numerical law for every colloid. For a positively charged sol, the relevant counter ions are anions instead; chloride, sulfate and phosphate cannot be ranked by the cation attached to them alone. Changes in p H or complexation can alter particle charge and invalidate a simple comparison. Identify the measured endpoint, charge and concentration units before translating an observation into a coagulation argument.
points: Negative sol · Cations oppose particle charge · Counter-ions are positive
Thresholds: Na 50; Mg 1; Al 0.1 mM · Lower threshold is stronger · Relative power 1 : 50 : 500
Positive sol · Anions oppose particle charge · Reassess ions and conditions

board.heading: Coagulation evidence starts with the colloid charge

chapters.title: Choose an indicator from the equivalence region
chapters.formula: Strong/strong: near pH 7 at 25 °C; weak acid/strong base: above 7
chapters.script: Indicator selection follows the titration curve rather than a rule that every equivalence point has p H seven. For an ordinary dilute strong acid and strong base titration at twenty five degrees Celsius, equivalence is near neutral. A weak acid titrated by a strong base instead leaves its conjugate base in solution, so hydrolysis makes the equivalence solution basic. A weak base titrated by a strong acid leaves a conjugate acid and gives an acidic equivalence solution. Choose an indicator whose transition lies within the steep p H change for the actual concentration and system. Phenolphthalein is commonly suitable for a typical ethanoic acid and sodium hydroxide titration, while methyl orange would change too early in that comparison. This is not a guarantee that one named indicator works at every dilution. The observed colour endpoint is also not identical by definition to the stoichiometric equivalence point. For a weak acid with supplied p K a four point seven six, the ideal half equivalence buffer has equal acid and conjugate base amounts, giving p H four point seven six. Half equivalence and equivalence therefore answer different questions.
points: Strong acid / strong base; 25 °C · Matched dilute system · Equivalence near pH 7
Weak acid / strong base · Conjugate base hydrolysis · Equivalence above 7; suitable basic indicator
Weak acid; half equivalence · [A⁻]=[HA] in ideal buffer · pH=pKa; not equivalence pH

board.heading: Choose an indicator from the equivalence region

chapters.title: Two carbonate endpoints separate a mixture
chapters.formula: Carbonate + bicarbonate only: n(CO₃²⁻)=cVP; n(HCO₃⁻)=c(VT−2VP)
chapters.script: A two endpoint acid titration can distinguish carbonate from bicarbonate when the sample composition is restricted appropriately. Assume the only acid consuming bases are carbonate and bicarbonate. At the first idealized endpoint, carbonate has accepted one proton to become bicarbonate. The acid amount used to that stage therefore equals the initial carbonate amount. At the total second endpoint, each initial carbonate has accepted two protons and each initial bicarbonate one. If the same acid concentration is used, the initial bicarbonate amount equals concentration times the total volume minus twice the first endpoint volume. Use litres for volumes. For zero point one zero zero molar acid, a first endpoint at ten point zero zero millilitres and a total endpoint at twenty six point zero zero correspond to one point zero zero millimole carbonate and zero point six zero zero millimole bicarbonate. The second stage alone consumes sixteen millilitres, which is different from the total twenty six. A negative calculated bicarbonate amount flags a failed assumption or inconsistent data in this restricted model. Other bases, dissolved carbon dioxide behaviour and endpoint uncertainty require separate treatment in real analysis.
points: Only CO₃²⁻ and HCO₃⁻ consume acid · First endpoint: one H⁺ per CO₃²⁻ · n(CO₃²⁻)=cVP
Total endpoint from original reading · Two H⁺ / carbonate; one / bicarbonate · n(HCO₃⁻)=c(VT−2VP)
c=0.100 M; VP=10.00; VT=26.00 mL · Carbonate 1.00 mmol · Bicarbonate 0.600 mmol

chapters.title: An aliquot result must be scaled to the whole sample
chapters.formula: Whole-sample analyte = aliquot analyte × total solution volume / aliquot volume
chapters.script: A titration measures the analyte in the portion actually transferred to the flask. To report the whole sample amount, restore any dilution and aliquot factors explicitly. Suppose a one point zero zero zero gram sample is completely dissolved and made to two hundred fifty point zero millilitres, with all relevant iron present as iron two. A twenty five point zero zero millilitre aliquot consumes ten point zero zero millilitres of zero point zero two zero zero molar permanganate in the stipulated acidic iron two titration. The permanganate amount is zero point two zero zero millimole. The one to five ratio gives one point zero zero millimole iron in that aliquot. The volumetric flask contains ten such aliquots, so the whole sample contains ten point zero millimoles iron. Using the supplied rounded iron molar mass of fifty six grams per mole, this is zero point five six zero gram iron, or fifty six point zero percent by mass. The result assumes quantitative transfer, complete reaction and no interfering reductants. The flask volume scales the measured amount; it does not replace the aliquot volume in the original reaction stoichiometry.

250.0 mL flask; 25.00 mL aliquot · Scale factor 250.0/25.00=10 · 10.0 mmol Fe in whole sample
Fe=56 g/mol; sample=1.000 g · Mass Fe=0.560 g · 56.0% Fe; no interfering reductants

chapters.title: Iodine-clock time measures a fixed conversion threshold
chapters.formula: I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻; at fixed threshold, average rate ∝ 1/t
chapters.script: An iodine clock separates formation of a species from the later appearance of a visible signal. In a suitable acidic iodide and peroxide system, iodine is produced while added thiosulfate consumes it. One iodine molecule reacts with two thiosulfate ions. The familiar starch colour becomes persistent only when the scavenger is exhausted and iodine species can accumulate. A delayed colour therefore does not mean that no iodine was formed earlier. For an idealized initial thiosulfate amount of one point zero zero millimole, exhaustion corresponds to zero point five zero zero millimole iodine consumed by that reaction. If two otherwise comparable mixtures have the same total volume and threshold but times of forty and twenty seconds, the second has twice the average iodine formation rate to the threshold. This is an average over the induction interval, not automatically an instantaneous rate constant. Inferring a reaction order also requires knowing which concentration changed while other conditions were held fixed. Temperature, mixing, reagent volumes and scavenger amount can all change the time. Keep a fixed conversion threshold before using reciprocal time as a rate proxy.
points: Iodine forms before persistent colour · Thiosulfate consumes I₂ in 2:1 ratio · No colour does not mean no reaction

Same threshold and volume; 40 s → 20 s · Average formation rate doubles · 1/t proxy is not itself rate constant

chapters.title: Gravimetry converts precipitate mass into analyte mass
chapters.formula: n(SO₄²⁻)=m(BaSO₄,corrected)/M(BaSO₄); sulfate mass is not precipitate mass
chapters.script: A gravimetric precipitate contains the analyte plus atoms supplied by the precipitating reagent. In a supplied sulfate analysis, a zero point six zero zero zero gram sample gives a measured barium sulfate mass zero point four seven one zero gram. A matched additive blank contributes zero point zero zero five zero gram, leaving corrected precipitate mass zero point four six six zero. Use the supplied rounded barium sulfate molar mass two hundred thirty three grams per mole. The corrected precipitate represents zero point zero zero two zero zero zero mole sulfate, since each formula unit contains one sulfate. Multiplying by the sulfate molar mass ninety six gives zero point one nine two gram sulfate, or thirty two point zero percent of the original sample. Calling the entire precipitate mass sulfate would count the added barium as analyte. This result assumes the isolated material has the stated composition, quantitative recovery and a valid blank correction. Retained liquid or coprecipitated material can bias mass upward, whereas incomplete precipitation or transfer loss can bias it downward. A larger recovered mass does not automatically demonstrate a more accurate analysis.

chapters.title: Silver halides need colour and ammonia behaviour together
chapters.formula: AgCl: white, dissolves in dilute NH₃; AgBr: cream, requires concentrated NH₃ in the usual comparison; AgI: yellow, remains
chapters.script: A silver halide comparison combines precipitation with complex formation rather than relying only on colour. In the standard introductory comparison under a controlled analytical scheme, silver chloride is white and dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia. Silver bromide is cream and is much less soluble in dilute ammonia, while concentrated ammonia can dissolve it under the usual comparison conditions. Silver iodide is yellow and remains essentially undissolved in that concentrated ammonia comparison. Ammonia binds dissolved silver ions as a diamminesilver complex, lowering the free silver concentration and allowing more solid to dissolve when the combined equilibria permit. The differing silver halide solubilities mean that the same ligand does not produce the same observation for all three. These are qualitative comparison conditions, not claims of absolute zero solubility or a universal endpoint independent of concentration. Mixtures, lighting, small precipitate amounts and interfering ions can make colour alone misleading. Earlier clean extract and acid choice controls still apply. The observation should refer to the defined precipitate and reagent stage, rather than treating every pale solid that responds to ammonia as an infallible identity test.

In suitable excess sodium hydroxide, the amphoteric aluminium hydroxide dissolves through formation of soluble hydroxoaluminate, commonly written as the tetrahydroxoaluminate ion in this aqueous model. The sulfite ion consumes two protons to give sulfur dioxide and water; with the barium ion released, the full precipitate equation balances both atoms and total charge. Gas identity is inferred through a controlled scheme, never by tasting or deliberately smelling it. Oxidation of sulfite to sulfate before observation can change the result, and mixtures require additional separation. Keep the original anion, the precipitate and the acid reaction as distinct stages. A persistent barium precipitate is supporting evidence under specified conditions, not a complete analysis of an arbitrary unknown sample.

chapters.title: Ammonium evidence follows proton transfer without changing nitrogen oxidation state
chapters.formula: NH₄⁺+OH⁻→NH₃+H₂O; liberated basic gas is evidence within a controlled salt-analysis scheme
chapters.script: Ammonium identification begins with an acid base change rather than a nitrogen oxidation reaction. In the standard analytical model, ammonium ion reacts with hydroxide to form ammonia and water. Nitrogen, hydrogen, oxygen and total charge all balance, and nitrogen remains at oxidation state minus three in both ammonium and ammonia. The ammonium ion carries charge plus one, whereas the ammonia molecule is neutral; a charge change of the species does not by itself imply oxidation. A supplied observation that liberated gas turns moist red litmus blue is consistent with a basic gas such as ammonia. Moisture matters because the indicator response requires the aqueous acid base environment. That one response is not unique proof for every possible unknown, since other volatile bases can interfere. Within a controlled inorganic salt scheme, sample blanks and exclusion of interfering species make the ammonium interpretation stronger. Nitrate does not simply become ammonia by this same hydroxide proton transfer equation; such a transformation would require additional reduction chemistry. Treat the gas observation and balanced equation as connected pieces of evidence, without inventing a reducing reagent or identifying a substance by its smell.

chapters.title: Flame observations need a clean blank and a separate confirmation
chapters.formula: Selected flame comparisons: Ca brick red; Ba apple green; sodium contamination can dominate yellow emission
chapters.script: A flame test is an emission observation, not a precipitate test or a direct oxidation state measurement. In the elementary comparison, calcium gives a brick red flame and barium an apple green flame under appropriate test conditions. Heating populates excited states, and emitted light appears as those species return to lower energy states. The familiar classroom colour does not imply one single visible wavelength or a unique spectrum from every compound in every flame. Sodium contamination can contribute a strong yellow signal, so an unclean support or reagent can obscure the sample response. A blank using the same support and reagents helps determine whether a colour comes from the test sample. Mixtures may show overlapping signals, and a weak or absent visible colour is not proof that every relevant ion is absent. For a calcium or barium identification, combine the flame comparison with a separate controlled chemical confirmation from the correct aliquot. These are interpretations of supplied observations rather than instructions for conducting a flame experiment. Do not treat colour names as sufficient evidence to infer concentration or sample purity.

chapters.title: Nitrite and nitrate have different oxidation ledgers with permanganate
chapters.script: Nitrite and nitrate contain the same element but do not have the same oxidation state or reducing capacity. Nitrogen in nitrite is plus three, while nitrogen in nitrate is plus five. In a selected acidic oxidation, each nitrite ion releases two electrons as it becomes nitrate. A permanganate ion reduced to manganese two accepts five electrons. Ten electrons are matched by five nitrites and two permanganates. The complete net balance uses six protons and gives three waters along with five nitrates and two manganese two ions. Under this stipulated quantitative endpoint, zero point zero one zero mole of nitrite requires zero point zero zero four mole of permanganate. Nitrate already contains nitrogen at plus five and does not supply the same nitrite to nitrate oxidation equivalents. A colour change with permanganate is still not uniquely diagnostic of nitrite, because many other reducing species also react. Actual acidic nitrite can undergo competing changes, so the net equation alone does not validate an assay procedure. The calculation assumes the stated products, complete reaction and controlled interference. Check both the electron count and the nitrogen inventory before interpreting a result.

chapters.title: Permanganate decolourization is oxidation evidence rather than unique proof of an alkene
chapters.formula: A C=C bond can be oxidized; aldehydes and other reductants can also consume MnO4−
chapters.script: A qualitative observation supports a chemical hypothesis only when alternative causes have been considered. Loss of permanganate colour can be consistent with oxidation of a carbon carbon double bond under the selected conditions. It does not uniquely prove that an unknown is an alkene. An aldehyde is also readily oxidized in suitable permanganate chemistry, even when it has no carbon carbon double bond. Other reducing substances or contamination may consume the reagent as well. Conversely, poor mixing, a poorly soluble sample or unsuitable conditions can make an expected change difficult to observe. A negative result is therefore meaningful only within a validated test domain. A useful reasoning table compares a reagent blank, a known positive control and the unknown under matched conditions, then asks what independent structural evidence distinguishes the remaining candidates. The manganese product also depends on the medium; a neutral or alkaline comparison cannot automatically use the acidic five-electron reduction to manganese two. Do not infer a numerical amount of unsaturation from colour loss without a specified stoichiometric endpoint and validated selectivity. This chapter separates an observation, an oxidation interpretation and a molecular identification, rather than treating those as the same claim.

quiz.question: For free [Mg2+]=.0100 M, Ksp(Mg(OH)2)=10⁻¹¹ and Kw=10⁻¹⁴, the ideal onset pH is:
Pure monoprotic KHP .5105 g, M=204.2 g/mol, consumes 25.00 mL NaOH. The standardized NaOH concentration is:
quiz.explanation: KHP amount=.002500 mol; the 1:1 neutralization gives CNaOH=.002500/.02500=.1000 M.

quiz.question: A pure diprotic acid sample .2500 g consumes 20.00 mL of that .1000 M base at complete two-proton equivalence. Its molar mass is:
quiz.explanation: The base amount is .002000 mol, so acid amount is half that; M=.2500/.001000=250 g/mol.

quiz.question: Back titration adds .02500 mol HCl and finds .007500 mol residual strong acid. Hydrogen ions consumed by the sample are:
quiz.explanation: Subtract amounts: .02500−.007500=.01750 mol H+ consumed.

quiz.question: If only CaCO3 consumes that .01750 mol H+ in a 1.000 g sample, using MCaCO3=100 g/mol, purity is:
quiz.explanation: Each carbonate consumes two protons; .008750 mol corresponds to .8750 g or 87.5% of the sample.

quiz.question: In the usual controlled silver-halide comparison, the precipitate readily dissolved by dilute aqueous ammonia is:
quiz.explanation: Complex formation permits AgCl dissolution under the standard dilute-ammonia comparison; AgBr requires different conditions and AgI remains.

quiz.question: Which combined observation is consistent with AgI in that comparison?
options: White and dissolves readily in dilute ammonia
Cream and always completely soluble in water
Yellow and remains in the concentrated-ammonia comparison
quiz.explanation: Use both the stated colour and ammonia behaviour, with interference controls.

quiz.question: The soluble aluminium species in the supplied excess-OH− model is:
quiz.explanation: Al(OH)3+OH−→[Al(OH)4]− balances atoms and charge while Al remains +3.

quiz.question: Why does excess-alkali dissolution alone not uniquely prove Al³⁺ in an arbitrary unknown?
options: Zinc hydroxide can also show amphoteric dissolution
Iron must disappear in every solution
quiz.explanation: The response distinguishes a specified pair but is shared by other ions, requiring separation and confirmation.

quiz.question: Acid reaction of the supplied BaSO₃ precipitate produces the gas:
quiz.explanation: BaSO3+2H+→Ba2++SO2+H2O. The sulfur oxidation state remains +4 in this acid-base conversion.

quiz.question: A white barium precipitate that persists in the specified usual dilute-acid comparison is consistent with:
options: A proof of every anion in a mixture
quiz.explanation: BaSO4 persistence supports sulfate under the defined scheme; one observation is not a complete arbitrary-mixture analysis.

quiz.question: In NH₄⁺+OH⁻→NH₃+H₂O, the nitrogen oxidation state:
quiz.explanation: Both NH4+ and NH3 have nitrogen−3; this is proton transfer, not reduction.

quiz.question: Why does a basic liberated gas turning moist red litmus blue need additional context?
options: Every basic gas is uniquely ammonium
Nitrate automatically releases NH₃ with no reduction
quiz.explanation: The observation is consistent with ammonia but needs the controlled scheme and interference exclusions.

quiz.question: In the supplied Ni2+ dimethylglyoxime balance, how many monoanionic bidentate ligands form one neutral chelate?
quiz.explanation: Two charges of−1 balance Ni2+; two nitrogen donors per ligand give four donors.

quiz.question: Ideal ligand amount needed for1.00 mmol Ni2+ in Ni(Hdmg)2?
quiz.explanation: The selected chelate has two ligand units per nickel ion; suitable precipitation conditions are still required.

quiz.question: Why can suitable strong-acid conditions dissolve calcium oxalate?
options: Calcium must be reduced to metal
Protonation lowers free oxalate dianion and favours dissolution
quiz.explanation: The solubility equilibrium responds to removal of free C2O4^2− by protonation.

quiz.question: An ideal.50 mmol calcium oxalate precipitate contains what calcium amount?
options: Its white colour alone fixes the amount
quiz.explanation: CaC2O4 has one calcium per formula unit; a measured precipitate amount is distinct from an uncalibrated visual colour.

quiz.question: Which ordered flame comparison is correct under the selected classroom conditions: calcium, barium?
quiz.explanation: These are selected emission colours, not unique identifications or precipitate colours.

quiz.question: A yellow flame also appears in the support-and-reagent blank. Best inference?
options: The sample must contain only calcium
Contamination such as sodium may contribute, so the sample signal needs discrimination
The sample is proven pure sodium chloride
quiz.explanation: A blank shows a source independent of the sample; a separate confirmation is needed.

quiz.question: Which selected reagent system supports a yellow phosphomolybdate phosphate confirmation?
options: Ammonium molybdate in suitable nitric-acid medium
quiz.explanation: The named reagent and medium define this phosphate comparison; colour alone is insufficient.

quiz.question: Does a visible positive orthophosphate test automatically quantify total phosphorus in any organic sample?
options: No; speciation, prior conversion and calibration must be established
Yes; all phosphorus forms give an identical calibrated colour
Yes; yellow intensity gives concentration without standards
Yes; any yellow solid is pure phosphate
quiz.explanation: The qualitative response is specific to the stated test conditions and measured species, not a universal total-phosphorus assay.

quiz.question: With [S2−]=10−27/[H+]², what is [S2−] at pH1 in the supplied model?
quiz.explanation: At pH1, [H+]=10−1 M; division by 10−2 gives 10−25 M.

quiz.question: Initial [Cu2+]=[Zn2+]=.001 M; supplied Ksp values are10−36 and10−24. At [S2−]=10−25 M, which initial onset is crossed?
quiz.explanation: Both ion products are10−28; this exceeds10−36 for CuS but remains below10−24 for ZnS.

quiz.question: For the stated acidic nitrite-to-nitrate and permanganate-to-Mn2+ endpoints, .010 mol nitrite requires:
quiz.explanation: Five nitrites release ten electrons and two permanganates accept ten; .010×2/5=.004 mol.

quiz.question: Why does nitrate not supply the same reducing equivalents as nitrite in this selected oxidation?
options: N is already+5 in nitrate rather than+3
Every nitrate is an insoluble solid
Nitrate has more negative total charge
quiz.explanation: Nitrite nitrogen rises from+3 to+5; nitrate nitrogen is already+5 and does not undergo that same oxidation.

quiz.question: In the displayed dichromate-to-chromyl-chloride map, chromium changes from:
quiz.explanation: O(−2) and Cl(−1) place chromium at+6 in CrO2Cl2, as it is in dichromate.

quiz.question: With .004 mol available chloride, the formal maximum CrO2Cl2 amount in the selected balance is:
quiz.explanation: Four chloride ions give two chromyl chloride molecules, so the formal ceiling is .004×2/4=.002 mol.

quiz.question: Which conclusion from permanganate colour loss alone is justified in the selected test context?
options: Every original C=C has been counted quantitatively
The sample contains only one compound
An oxidizable species may be present; identity needs more evidence
quiz.explanation: Alkenes are not the only species that consume permanganate; aldehydes and other reductants can also respond.

quiz.question: Why must a neutral/alkaline permanganate comparison specify its manganese product before a mole calculation?
options: The electron capacity depends on the stated manganese endpoint
All manganese products have the same oxidation state
The acidic Mn2+ ratio applies in every medium
Colour alone gives the exact number of electrons
quiz.explanation: MnO4− to Mn2+ accepts five electrons, whereas a MnO2 endpoint accepts three; the medium and selected products matter.
